title: AI document processing: how accurate is it on financial documents?
description: We benchmarked AI tools on 30 fund reports, with answers locked in advance. Which ones made no mistakes, what each costs per report, and how to set it up.
summary: AI document processing reads a page's text like OCR does, then labels which value is which, such as the total or due date[^3][^4]. Plain OCR (text recognition) stops at raw text[^2][^3]. Start with the document your team re-keys most: reading costs cents, and staff time is the real cost[^5][^1].
humanRole: Reviewer, someone who knows the documents: settles every fact the two models disagree on.[^5] The reviewer can override any AI value.[^17][^23]
Team lead: sets the error rate the team will accept and signs off before go-live. NIST says people, not the tool, should set those limits.[^23]
Approver, not the person who fixed the value: releases facts that feed money or reports into the system others rely on.[^24] Small teams that can't split duties can use other checks.[^24]
Every reviewer checks the quoted page, not just the number.[^31] The EU AI Act names the risk of leaning on AI output: automation bias.[^17]
teamAfter: Checking replaces typing. Checking was already part of the job: O*NET lists comparing data with source documents as a core data-entry task.[^26]
Disagreements become the main work: in our test, about 1 fact in 4 went to a person.[^5]
New staff get up to speed faster. In a study of 5,172 support agents, those two months in with AI help matched agents six months in without it.[^27]
Time back for harder cases: workers who use generative AI report saving 5.4% of their hours, about 2.2 hours a week.[^28] Among US firms using AI, 66% use it only to help staff.[^25]
verdict: Have two models from different vendors read each file; a person settles their disagreements[^9][^10].
AI reading costs cents per report; staff time and errors are the real cost[^5][^1].
Best two models: zero mistakes on our 30 fund reports; the true rate may still be 1 report in 10[^5][^13].
First step: benchmark two models on 50 files from one team's queue[^14][^23].

pickElse: Thousands of standard invoices a day? A prebuilt cloud parser, a ready-made reader for standard forms, costs about a penny a page[^2][^4].

Your files cannot leave your network: run an open-source model on your own servers. Expect more wrong values: in our first round the two local models made 8 each, where Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5 made none[^5].
You only need searchable text, not fields: basic text recognition (OCR) costs well under a penny a page at all three big clouds[^2][^3][^4].

ownData.title: Which AI made the fewest mistakes on 30 fund reports?
ownData.intro: GPT-6.2 Sol (OpenAI) and Gemini 4 Hydrogen (Google) made zero mistakes each on FinExtractBench, our own test of 30 public private-fund reports[^5]. The reports run 781 pages, and we wrote and locked every right answer by hand before any tool ran[^5]. Each tool read each raw PDF once; a mistake is a wrong value or a value the report never states.
rows: Gemini 4 Carbon (Google; a weaker model, for comparison)
ownData.note: Limits: one person wrote the answers, and the reports are digital, in English and 56 pages at most[^5]. Zero mistakes in 30 reports still allows a true rate of up to about 1 report in 10[^13]. Re-run on 10 reports as scanned page images, both tools still made 0 mistakes[^5].

example.input: A 57-page quarterly report from a private equity fund, as a PDF.
example.output: Money committed (commitment), money paid in (paid-in capital), money paid back out (distributions), and what the fund is worth today (NAV, net asset value). Each fact comes with its page number and the exact words it came from. Any fact the two models disagree on is flagged.

howToTest: Record today's baseline first: staff minutes per file, and errors that reach the systems and reports downstream.

Pick 50 real files from one team's queue, including your worst scans and longest reports, plus facts some files never state, to catch invented answers. Even vendors advise benchmarking on your own documents[^14].
Write the right answer for every fact before any AI reads the files, and lock it, so the AI's output cannot sway it.
Require each answer to name its page and quote the exact words, and have code check that the quote is there.
Count wrong answers apart from blanks. A blank goes to a person; a wrong number can slip through.
Report minutes, wrong fields and cost per file, before and after; multiply the change by monthly volume to price it in dollars. Run the winner again on new files before you go live.

buyVsBuild.buy: Buy a prebuilt parser or an accounts payable tool when your files are standard invoices, receipts or IDs. The big clouds' prebuilt models already cover those[^2][^4]. Buying fits best when you mainly need volume and an audit trail.
buyVsBuild.build: Build on frontier models (the newest, most capable ones) when your files are unique to your business and a wrong number is expensive. The build is a prompt, a fact list, a checker and a review queue where your team settles about 2 facts per report[^5]. If files must stay in-house, run an open-source model on your own servers; in our benchmark, local models made more wrong values[^5].

watchOuts: Vendor accuracy numbers mostly come from the vendor's own benchmark runs[^14], and public answer keys have errors too[^12]. Even on our locked-answer set, when the AI and our key differed, the AI was right in 22 of 57 cases, so check your key[^5].
A model that writes a plausible wrong number is worse than one that leaves the field blank[^11]. Score them separately.
Two tables on one page with similar labels fooled 7 of 10 tools in our hard round[^5]. Check the facts that sit near look-alikes.
Prices and model versions change: Mistral's newer OCR model costs twice its older one[^6]. Re-run your benchmark when either changes, and keep the files and answers so the re-run is cheap.
Read the vendor's data terms. Datalab's rate card shows prices with a 25% discount that assumes you let it train on your data[^7].
Plan reviewer time: in our benchmark, about 1 fact in 4 (66 of 270) went to a person[^5]. Multiply by the facts you pull each month to size the workload.

faq.q: What is the difference between OCR and AI document processing?
faq.a: OCR turns a page into raw text, while document AI also knows which number is which, like the total or the due date.[^2][^3][^4] Use OCR alone when you only need searchable text.[^2]

faq.q: How accurate is AI document processing?
faq.a: AI document processing is very accurate on clean files: on our 30 fund reports, the two best models made no mistakes.[^5] Accuracy still depends on your documents, so test on your own.[^23][^14] Zero in 30 still allows a true rate of up to about 1 in 10.[^13]

Yes, but accuracy drops on scans. In a 2025 study, the best model got 96.5% of invoice fields right on clean files and 92.7% on scanned ones.[^29] Re-run on 10 of our reports as scanned images, both top tools still made no mistakes.[^5]

faq.q: Is it safe to send company documents to an AI model?
faq.a: Only under business or API (application programming interface) terms you have read: OpenAI and Anthropic say they do not train on that data by default.[^30][^31] OpenAI may keep API data up to 30 days to spot abuse, unless you qualify for zero retention.[^30]

faq.q: Will AI document processing replace data entry staff?
faq.a: Not entirely: AI changes the job from typing to checking, though fewer keying jobs are projected.[^26][^32] Among US firms using AI, 66% use it only to help staff, and AI-related employment fell in 2%.[^25] BLS still projects data entry keyer jobs to fall 25.5% by 2035.[^32]

sources.name: Xiong et al., Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? (2023)
sources.what: Finds that language models tend to be overconfident when they state their own confidence.

sources.name: Cohen et al., LM vs LM (EMNLP 2023)
sources.what: Having a second model question the first catches factual errors better than earlier methods, often by a large gap.

sources.name: Manakul et al., SelfCheckGPT (EMNLP 2023)
sources.what: Facts that disagree across several answers to the same question are likely invented; consistent facts are likely true.

sources.name: OpenAI, Why language models hallucinate (2025)
sources.what: Argues errors are worse than abstentions and evaluations should penalise confident errors more than uncertainty.

sources.name: Northcutt et al., Pervasive label errors in test sets (2021)
sources.what: Finds at least 3.3% wrong answers on average across 10 widely used benchmark answer keys.

sources.name: Newman, JAMA 1995, interpreting small numerators
sources.what: With zero events in N trials, the upper 95% confidence limit for the true rate is about 3/N.

sources.name: EU AI Act, Annex III
sources.what: Lists credit scoring of people and life and health insurance pricing as high-risk uses.

sources.name: EU AI Act, Article 12
sources.what: High-risk AI systems must automatically record events (logs) over their lifetime.

sources.name: EU AI Act, Article 14
sources.what: High-risk AI systems must let people oversee them, stay aware of over-relying on output (automation bias), and disregard, override or reverse it.

sources.name: Council of the EU, AI omnibus final approval (30 Jun 2026)
sources.what: Rules for stand-alone high-risk AI systems now apply from 2 December 2027.

sources.name: Lewis Silkin, Digital Omnibus on AI in force (Jul 2026)
sources.what: The omnibus defers Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027.

sources.name: 12 CFR 1002.9 (Cornell LII)
sources.what: Adverse action notices must give specific principal reasons; citing a failed score alone is not enough.

sources.name: CFPB Circular 2022-03
sources.what: Explained that creditors using complex algorithms must still give the specific principal reasons for a denial; withdrawn as guidance on 12 May 2025.

sources.name: NYDFS Circular Letter No. 7 (2024)
sources.what: Insurers stay responsible for vendor AI tools in underwriting and pricing and should seek audit rights in vendor contracts.

sources.name: NIST, AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 (NIST AI 100-1, Jan 2023)
sources.what: "Accuracy measurements should always be paired with clearly defined and realistic test sets... representative of conditions of expected use." Human judgment should set metric thresholds; monitoring plans should include appeal and override.

sources.name: US GAO, Green Book (2025), Principle 10
sources.what: Segregation of duties separates authorizing, processing and recording, and reviewing "so that no one individual controls all key aspects of a transaction." Where staff are too few, design alternative controls.

sources.name: US Census Bureau, CES-WP-26-25, The Microstructure of AI Diffusion (Apr 2026)
sources.what: "Most users (66%) rely on AI solely to augment tasks, while AI-related employment decreases are rare, occurring in only 2% of firms." Document analysis is a leading task use.

sources.what: Study of 5,172 support agents: AI help raised issues resolved per hour by 15%. Agents two months in with AI performed like agents over six months in without it.

sources.what: Nationally representative survey: generative AI users saved 5.4% of work hours on average, about 2.2 hours in a 40-hour week.

offer.heading: Not sure which AI to trust with your documents? Get a free diagnostic
offer.body: Bring us one document type, your monthly volume and what a wrong number costs you. In 30 minutes you leave with the first step and a before-and-after measure, in writing.

reviews.notes: Wanted to see who does what before the benchmark. On this page now leads with who checks, overrides and signs off, and follows the page order. The bottom line said the true rate may be "1 in 10" without saying of what; it now says 1 report in 10.

Tripped on OCR and "system of record". OCR is now defined as text recognition where it first appears, and the approver bullet and recipe 2 now name the system in plain words (accounting, CRM or reporting). Frontier models, NAV and maker-checker were already defined.

Asked whether one unit can pilot first and what it is worth. The test now pulls its 50 files from one team's queue, and the last step turns the change per file into dollars a month. The first bottom-line step already said one team's queue.

The head of document operations checked the control blocks. Recipe 2 said "your finance or ops checker"; it now says your reviewer decides and a second person approves, so it reads for any document team. The approver step applies only where facts feed money or reports, to keep review time sane.

Looked for what it costs, whether the files are safe and what happens to staff. The FAQ now answers data privacy from the vendors' own terms and jobs from Census and BLS. The offer now asks for one document type and monthly volume and promises the first step and a before-and-after measure in writing.

rules.name: EU AI Act, Annex III
rules.what: Reading documents is not a high-risk use on its own. It becomes part of one when the facts feed credit scoring of people or life and health insurance pricing[^15]. Then logging and human oversight apply[^16][^17], from 2 December 2027[^18][^19].

rules.name: Regulation B, 12 CFR 1002.9
rules.what: If extracted facts feed a US credit decision, a decline still needs specific reasons[^20], even when an algorithm made it[^20][^33]. The CFPB withdrew its 2022 circular on algorithm declines in May 2025, but the rule itself still applies[^33][^21]. A wrongly read fact becomes a wrong reason, so keep the page and quote behind every fact.

rules.name: NYDFS Circular Letter No. 7
rules.what: New York insurers that use AI in underwriting and pricing stay responsible for vendor tools[^22]. Where available, their vendor contracts should give them audit rights[^22].

answers.example: AI pulls out the fund's commitment, paid-in capital, distributions and NAV (net asset value), each with its page number and the exact words it came from[^5].
answers.recipes: A person should check only the exceptions: the facts whose quote fails the code check or where two models disagree, about 1 fact in 4 in our benchmark[^5].
answers.rules: Three rules can apply: the EU AI Act when extracted facts feed credit scoring or insurance pricing, US Regulation B for credit declines, and New York's DFS guidance for insurers[^15][^20][^22]. Reading documents is not high-risk on its own; the rules bite when the facts feed those decisions[^15].
answers.benchmark: Lock the right answers for 50 of your own files first, run each tool on them, make every answer quote its page, and count wrong values apart from blanks[^14][^11].
answers.what-goes-wrong: Not on their own: most vendor accuracy numbers come from the vendor's own benchmark runs, so test on your own files[^14]. Public answer keys have errors too[^12].
answers.buy-or-build: Buy a prebuilt parser for standard invoices, receipts or IDs, and build on frontier models when your files are unique and a wrong number is expensive[^2][^4][^5].
answers.something-else: Pick something other than a frontier model when you read thousands of standard invoices a day, when files cannot leave your network, or when searchable text is enough[^2][^4][^5][^3]. Use a prebuilt cloud parser, a local open-source model or plain OCR, respectively[^2][^5][^3].
answers.human-role: Your team keeps three calls: a reviewer settles facts the models disagree on, a team lead sets the acceptable error rate, and a separate approver releases the facts[^5][^23][^24]. Any reviewer can override any AI value[^17][^23].
answers.team-after: After AI reads the documents, your team checks instead of typing and settles the facts the two models disagree on, about 1 in 4 in our test[^26][^5]. Staff also get time back for harder cases, about 2.2 hours a week for generative AI users[^28].
